result.markdown: --- title: "Delay differential equations" course-unit: a01-delay-differential-equations status: complete --- ## Why this unit matters - Every earlier model assumes an **exponentially distributed** infectious period: memoryless recovery at constant hazard $\gamma$. - A delay differential equation (DDE) replaces that with the opposite extreme: every infectious period lasts *exactly* $\tau$ time units. - Question: how much does the **shape**, not just the mean, of the infectious-period distribution change epidemic dynamics? ::: {.notes} Frame this as a direct challenge to the memoryless assumption baked into every ODE/CTMC/SDE model so far. The point is not that fixed delays are more "realistic" than exponential ones — real infectious periods sit between the two — but that the two extremes bound how sensitive predictions are to a modeling choice that is often made for mathematical convenience. ::: ## Model assumptions and classification Same baseline cohort throughout the course: $N=1000$, $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, $c=10$, $\beta=0.05$. Only the recovery mechanism changes. | Property | Classification | |---|---| | Determinism | Deterministic | | Time / state | Continuous / continuous | | Infectious period | Fixed delay $\tau = 1/\gamma = 4$ (variance 0) | Still **deterministic, continuous, population-level** — but *not* Markovian: the recovery flow at $t$ depends on the state at $t - \tau$. ## Equations $$ \frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\lambda(t) S(t), \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda(t) S(t) - \lambda(t-\tau) S(t-\tau), \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda(t-\tau) S(t-\tau) $$ with $\lambda(t) = \beta c\, I(t)/N(t)$ and history $h(t) = (N, 0, 0)$ for $t \le 0$: recovery at $t$ equals infection $\tau$ time units earlier. ::: {.notes} Emphasize that the history function is not optional bookkeeping — a DDE needs a *function* on $(-\infty, 0]$, not a single initial vector, because the right-hand side reaches back in time. ::: ## Method of steps - On $[0, \tau]$ the delayed term is fully known from the history $h$, so the DDE is an *ordinary* ODE there. - That segment's dense solution becomes the exact history for $[\tau, 2\tau]$, and so on — solving a sequence of ODEs. - Derivative discontinuities from the $t=0$ history mismatch propagate to $t = \tau, 2\tau, \dots$, smoothing at each step. - Declaring the lag via `constant_lags` tells the solver exactly where to place step boundaries instead of discovering them by trial and error. ## Julia API ```julia using DelayDiffEq, OrdinaryDiffEq function sir_dde!(du, u, h, p, t) S, I, R = u β, c, τ = p λ = β * c * I / (S + I + R) Sd, Id, Rd = h(p, t - τ) # delayed state λd = β * c * Id / (Sd + Id + Rd) du[1] = -λ * S du[2] = λ * S - λd * Sd du[3] = λd * Sd end prob = DDEProblem(sir_dde!, u0, history, tspan, p; constant_lags = [τ]) sol = solve(prob, MethodOfSteps(Tsit5()); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8) ``` `MethodOfSteps` wraps any `OrdinaryDiffEq` algorithm; `h(p, t)` supplies the delayed state as the third positional argument of the right-hand side. ## Generated result ::: {#cell-fig-slide-a01-trajectories .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-a01-trajectories .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Fixed-delay DDE (solid) vs exponential-recovery ODE (dashed) with the same mean infectious period τ = 1/γ = 4. ::: ::: ## Validation - **Cross-check**: an independent two-stage (presolved ODE + continued DDE) construction agrees with the single-history run to solver tolerance. - **Conservation & nonnegativity**: $S+I+R=1000$ and all states $\ge 0$ throughout $[0, 40]$. - **Structural comparison**: at matched mean infectious period, the fixed delay produces a **taller, sharper** peak ($\approx 351$) than exponential recovery ($\approx 158$) — the shape of the distribution matters, not just its mean. ## Interpretation and limitations - A fixed delay has coefficient of variation 0: nobody recovers early, so the initial cohort transmits at full strength for all of $[0, \tau)$. - Omitting `constant_lags` still gives a correct answer but forces the adaptive controller to *rediscover* breakpoints at $\tau, 2\tau, \dots$ — slower and less accurate near those points. - The "instant seeding" history convention (all $I(0)$ infected exactly at $t=0$) is convenient, not realistic; the two-stage construction shows how to relax it. - Still fully deterministic — no demographic noise. That gap motivates the stochastic delay differential equation of the next unit. ::: {.notes} If time allows, sketch why the linear-chain (Erlang) trick from the model-composition appendix is the usual way to interpolate between the two extremes without leaving the ODE framework — useful context for why DDEs are a specialized, not default, tool. ::: ## Key takeaways - DDEs model *fixed* recovery delays; the method of steps reduces them to a sequence of ODE solves. - Declare `constant_lags` for solver efficiency at known breakpoints. - Distribution *shape* (not just mean) materially changes epidemic peak height and timing. - This model has no stochasticity — see the next two units for the stochastic and individual-level extensions. ## Further reading - [DelayDiffEq.jl documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/DelayDiffEq/stable/) - [SciML DDE problem reference](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/types/dde_types/) - Full derivation, code, and exercises: [book chapter](../../appendices/01-delay-differential-equations.html)
